title: Call clips and trailer cutter
what_it_does: Pulls a recorded call from Fathom, finds the strongest moments in the transcript, cuts them on exact words with clean captions, and stitches them into clips or a two-minute trailer. Used to make the Humans V Robots: Amplified demo trailer and a Best Moments page of call highlights.
why: Great moments from calls were stuck inside hour-long recordings. Cutting them by hand meant scrubbing video and fighting Zoom's laggy burned-in captions.
integrations: Call recorder API key, to list calls and grab each video and transcript (Fathom)
A speech-to-text model with word timings, to cut on exact words (faster-whisper, free)
A video tool, to cut, caption and join clips (ffmpeg, free)
Cloud storage access, to share the finished video by link (Google Drive)
starter_prompt: I want to turn my recorded calls into short clips of the best moments. Before building anything, ask me: 1) where my calls are recorded (Fathom, Zoom, Otter) and whether it has an API or a download, 2) what counts as a great moment for me (a client win, a strong teaching line, an emotional peak), 3) where the finished clips should go. Then build the smallest working version: one script that takes one recording and its transcript, lists the 5 best moments with start and end times and a one-line reason, and cuts just the top one into a video file with captions. Show me that clip before adding a trailer or automation.

title: Alumni outreach CRM
what_it_does: A one-page CRM for personally reaching about 300 past students. Each person gets a card with a drafted message in their language, personalized with their name and what they built. One click opens WhatsApp with the text filled in, he records a voice note, and the card moves along the pipeline with today's date. A chat co-pilot answers "where did we leave off?" and flags anyone who hasn't replied in a week. A live counter shows how many he has sent today, a filter shows only people with a name on file, and cards without a name have a box for the name from their WhatsApp profile, plus a ready-to-copy contact label like "Maria (Nomad Cruise 17)". First day: 28 people contacted, 20 in one focused hour, against a target of 5 to 10.
why: He wanted to personally contact every alumnus in daily two-hour blocks, and keeping 300 conversations straight in his head and in WhatsApp wasn't going to work.
integrations: Spreadsheet access, to import the contact list (Google Sheets)
A place to host the page and save its data (Claude artifact, Cloudflare)
WhatsApp click-to-chat links, to open a chat with the message filled in (no API needed)
An AI chat, to draft personal messages and run the co-pilot (Claude)
starter_prompt: I want a simple CRM for reaching out personally to a list of people (past clients, alumni, leads). Before building anything, ask me: 1) where the list lives now and what I know about each person, 2) the one or two things every message should say, 3) which channel I reach them on (WhatsApp, email, Instagram). Then build one HTML page that loads my list as a CSV and shows a pipeline board (To contact, Contacted, Replied, Done). Each card shows a short personal draft using the person's name and notes, and a button that opens the chat with that text filled in. Clicking it stamps today's date and moves the card. Use 5 fake rows first, then my real list.

title: WhatsApp calendar assistant
what_it_does: Text a question on WhatsApp, like "am I free Thursday morning?" or "book a call with Ana at 3", and it answers from your Google Calendar or books the event. Twilio passes the message to a free Google Apps Script, Gemini works out what you mean, and the script reads or writes the calendar. It's the worked example for the AI Growth Session lesson on assistants.
why: He wanted an assistant that lives where he already types all day, and a build the group could copy with free tools.
integrations: A messaging bridge account, to pass messages to your code (Twilio for WhatsApp, or a Telegram bot, which needs no middleman)
A place for your code to run, with a public web address (Google Apps Script, free)
An LLM API key, to understand the request (Gemini free tier, Claude or OpenAI)
Calendar access, to read and book events (Google Calendar)
starter_prompt: I want a personal assistant I can text that answers questions about my calendar and books appointments. Before building anything, ask me: 1) where I want to text it (WhatsApp, Telegram, SMS), 2) which calendar I use, 3) what matters most to me: cheapest, easiest to set up, or most reliable. Then recommend one setup for the five boxes (where I type, bridge, where code runs, AI brain, calendar) and explain the trade-off in two lines. Build the smallest working version that answers one question, "what's on my calendar tomorrow?", and walk me through each setup step one at a time, waiting for me to confirm before the next.

title: Apartment hunt scorer
what_it_does: Searches three Colombian listing sites barrio by barrio, drops anything that fails his must-haves, checks real walking times to the nearest gym, work cafe and supermarket, and scores every place out of 100 with a one-line reason per line. A shared rating page shows each place with price, score breakdown, walk times and a small map, and opens on "Gems": the few places worth seeing the day they appear. Both people rate with stars and notes.
why: Hundreds of listings across several sites, most of them too small, too far from a gym or over budget once admin fees were added. Checking each one by hand ate evenings, and good owner-direct places went fast.
integrations: Public listing sites, searched with plain scripts (Finca Raiz, Metrocuadrado, Ciencuadras: no keys or logins)
A maps API key, for real walking times to the gym, cafe and supermarket (Google Maps Places + Distance Matrix)
An AI step, to judge workspace, terrace and nice-to-haves from each ad (Claude)
A page with a small shared database, for ratings and notes (Claude artifact)
Map tiles saved locally, because the page blocks outside images (OpenStreetMap)

starter_prompt: I want help finding a place to rent without checking every listing by hand. Before building anything, ask me: 1) the city, neighborhoods, move-in date and my all-in budget ceiling, 2) my must-haves (a place that fails one never shows up) and my nice-to-haves, 3) which listing sites people actually use there. Then build the smallest working version: one script that pulls listings from one site for one neighborhood, drops anything that fails my must-haves, and scores the rest out of 100 with a one-line reason per point. Show the top 10 on a simple page with price, score and a link. Research only: never contact landlords, log in or submit forms.
